text: TET-47 — ground what is owed, not everything
This design was built against a single pinned worktree, so every file range and command output cited below can be re-opened at that commit and read as this memo read it.
Where the brief is built today

The ticket's instruction to emit the full brief and a separate list of what to grade is not a matter of taste; it is the only shape the existing code permits without contradicting itself. `brief::build` maps every claim to a brief item with no filter, and its doc comment states in terms that a claim may not be dropped from the brief on account of what its evidence ledger already holds. An owed-scheduling feature that truncated the brief would have to delete that invariant first. Emitting the full brief and an adjacent list of owed ids leaves it intact.

The same signature decides where the new computation lives. `build` is handed claims and nothing else — no evidence records, no workspace identities — so owed-ness cannot be decided inside it. The owed list is computed by the caller that already loads the memo's records, and handed to the renderer alongside the items.
Rules 1 and 2 already exist under other names

`analyze_ledger` computes both of the first two owed conditions today. A claim with no evidence record at all lands in `ungrounded_claims`; a claim whose every digested record graded text it no longer carries lands in `out_of_proof`. The owed predicate takes those two sets as given rather than restating them, which keeps one definition of "graded on this wording" in the crate instead of two that can drift.

Rule 4 cannot be borrowed as cheaply, because `analyze_ledger` maintains two record sets that differ on exactly the case the floor is sensitive to. `fresh` requires the digest to equal the current proposition's; `grading_current` also admits records written before the digest field existed. Grandfathering is right where it lives — treating an undigested record as grading the current text makes the contradiction checks fire rather than fall silent — but a confirmation count is the opposite polarity. A pre-digest record counted as one of the N confirmations retires a claim from the schedule on evidence that may have graded other words entirely. The floor therefore counts `fresh` records only, and the design states that as a decision rather than inheriting it by accident.
The pin defect: compare, do not digest

The ticket asks whether the fix for the pin defect is to digest the pin or to compare it separately, and notes the two differ in what an existing ledger says afterwards. They differ decisively. Digesting the pin changes the value of `sha256_hex` for every claim that has one, so every record ever written would carry a digest no claim now matches, and `out_of_proof` — a machine failure — would fire across every existing memo at once, on wording nobody touched. Comparing separately has no such effect, and it is already possible: each record stores the pin it was graded against in a field the crate carries for fidelity and reads nowhere. The defect is not that the information is missing; it is that nothing looks at it. So the fix is a comparison, and it is answerable retroactively over ledgers written long before this design.

The channel itself is not what the ticket supposed. Asked to confirm that a claim's pin moves only when its citation list moves, the code says otherwise: nothing derives a claim's pin from the facts it cites. The pin is read out of the prose — a sentence of the form "at pin `<hash>`" sitting between the nearest heading and the ledger table — and the single value found there is stamped onto every claim in that table.

That makes rule 3 sharper than "pin changed", though not in the direction the ticket expected. Since one value covers the whole table, the condition is uniform across it: either every claim's graded pin still matches the memo's stated pin, or none does. Rule 3 is a re-pin detector for the document, and its practical effect is that re-pinning a memo to a new commit puts the entire ledger back on the schedule. That is the correct consequence — a pin is the tree the propositions were graded against — but it should be stated as such rather than discovered by an author who moved a pin and watched every claim reappear.

The stored pin is not a copy of the claim's pin, and that is what makes the comparison worth making. On the witnessed path a record's pin is the pin of the grounder's own fact — the tree that pass actually stood in — and the field's doc comment names the question it was written to make measurable: was this claim graded against the same tree the memo was written against? Rule 3 asks precisely that question. Implementing it as a comparison rather than a digest change also keeps every ledger written to date answerable, instead of invalidating all of them in one release.
The confirmation floor, and who counts as a witness

The floor needs a count of distinct non-author workspaces that have graded a wording, and the crate already computes one. `grounding_provenance` takes the claim's witnessed records, dedupes their `pass` values, reads the authoring workspace out of the snapshot's identity, and splits the result into how many of those workspaces authored the memo and how many did not. The second number is rule 4's input. Only one thing has to change: that count is taken over every record bearing the claim's id, with no attention to which wording each graded, and the floor must take it over the records matching the current wording alone.

There is a state in which the floor has no answer, and the doctrine that refusals are format-level rather than heuristic decides what to do in it. If the memo has no snapshot beside it, or a snapshot without an identity, nothing can say whether a grading workspace was the author's own — the existing report says as much in those two cases in those words. A floor computed anyway would be counting the author's self-grading as independent confirmation. So in those two states every claim stays owed under rule 4. That is not a guess about the missing file; it is a decision keyed on whether the file is there and parses, which is exactly the kind of condition the doctrine permits, and it errs toward scheduling rather than toward silent discharge.
The owed list must reach the pass that needs it

A grounding pass is handed a memo path and a workspace name and nothing else, on purpose, so `--owed` is only a viable surface if the memo carries everything the predicate reads. It does. The `check` driver already assembles exactly this set from the memo path: the claims and their pins out of the document, the records out of the evidence file beside it, and the authoring identity out of the snapshot directory beside that. It opens no authoring workspace. Nothing in the owed predicate is knowledge only the author has, so the grounder computes its own schedule from the same artifacts a reader could.
Rule 5: reuse the citation matcher, do not invent one

The ticket frames rule 5 as matching something like `C\d+` inside prose an author wrote, and worries about false positives. The crate has already answered both halves of that question for a different check. `citation_ids_in` is how the dependency cascade finds row-to-row edges inside a row's own free-text fields; it matches a bracketed id or a whole-line cites trailer, accepts any uppercase-led id carrying a digit or hyphen, and its documentation states that its failure mode is a false positive and never a missed citation, with two known collisions accepted rather than engineered around. A `C\d+` regex would be strictly worse on the axis the ticket cares about: it would miss ids of the shape this crate's own fixtures use, which is the false-negative direction, and it would give the codebase two different answers to the question of whether one row cites another.

One false negative survives, and it is stated rather than closed. A proposition mentioning another claim in bare prose, outside brackets, is not seen by the matcher, so its owed-ness does not propagate. Widening the pattern to catch it would fork the definition of a citation edge in two, and a stated bound beats an engineered-around one. An author who wants owed-ness to propagate through a proposition writes the reference the way the rest of the tool already expects to read it.

The closure's second half — that owed-ness propagates and so must iterate — is likewise a shape the crate has already built once. Check 5 indexes the reverse citation graph, then walks it breadth-first from each root with a visited set seeded by the root, precisely so that a citation cycling back terminates instead of looping. The owed closure is the same walk from a different seed: the claims owed by rules 1 through 4. What cannot be reused is the index. Check 5's graph is over rows and excludes ledger claims by design, and rule 5's edges are claim-to-claim, so the traversal is borrowed and the index is built fresh.
A schedule is not a termination condition

The ticket suspects that N=2 and the designer's rule to stop after the first round that provokes no revision may together prevent the loop from ever terminating on its intended signal, since the first round cannot leave nothing owed. They do not conflict, and the reason is in the stopping rules themselves: none of them makes the emptiness of a list an exit criterion. The loop ends when `check` is machine-clean and no live claim is refuted or unexplained, and the round-count rule keys on whether a round provoked a revision. The same section says in as many words that the human-owed partition is what you hand the reader, not a queue to empty. An owed list that is still non-empty when the loop stops means the run declined to spend another pass on it — which is a decision the author is entitled to make and the reader can see — not an obligation left undischarged.
Not a flag, and where the parameter goes

The ticket proposes `brief --owed [--confirm N]` and asks whether the owed behaviour should be a flag or the default, weighing it against the argument TET-46 used to reject `--include-tetel`. That argument transfers, and it decides more than the ticket asked. TET-46 rejected the flag because it would leave no trace in what the caller named, only in how they configured the call. A brief is the artifact independence rests on; two passes running `brief` on the same memo should not receive different documents because one of them typed an extra word. And there is nothing to trade away, because the owed section is additive — the full brief is emitted in either case, so no existing behaviour needs preserving. So `--owed` is not a flag: the brief always carries the owed list.

The floor itself stays a parameter, because the ticket's own measurement says it should be: N=2 retained five of seven discoveries and the remaining two are the argument for N=3 on a high-stakes memo. But a parameter is exactly the invisible configuration TET-46 objected to, so the value in force is printed in the brief beside the owed list. A reader of the brief, and a grounder acting on it, can then see which floor produced this schedule rather than having to know how the call was made.
What `check` prints, and what it declines to say

The ticket asks whether being under the floor is a finding at all, given that such a claim is scheduled rather than unsettled. It is not a finding, and the visibility requirement is met without making it one. The per-claim provenance line already names how many records were witnessed and in which workspaces, and prints as a bullet in the human-owed partition; it gains one more count, the number of distinct non-author workspaces that graded the wording the claim carries now. That is a count of records, which the doctrine permits, and it is the information a reader needs to judge how much independent reading a claim has had. What `check` does not do is compare that count to N. The floor is a scheduling parameter supplied to `brief`, and a comparison printed by `check` would turn a policy setting into a per-claim pronouncement — a document-level verdict assembled one claim at a time.

The blast radius of that extension is small enough to state exactly. `grounding_provenance` is named in three files across the whole worktree: the definition, field and zero-init in `checks.rs`, one call site in `lib.rs`, and one printing loop in `report.rs`. Nothing else — no test, no fixture — reads its wording, so the line can gain a count without any dependent needing to be found first.
What an implementer touches

Three symbols, each censused across the whole worktree. A new `owed_claims` occurs nowhere today, so the name is free. `render_text` gains the owed section and has one production caller and one unit test. `grounding_provenance` gains the confirmation count. One symbol is deliberately absent from that list: `BriefItem`. Its three-field shape is what withholds scope from a grounding pass, and no part of this design asks for a fourth field on it — the owed list travels beside the items, not inside them.
Borrowing the traversal, and the premises that came with it
The one mechanism this design copies
The premises the donor states, answered at the destination
why: P33 was created as an L3 heading and landed between the check section and the implementer section; a new L2 (P34) now opens the section, so this heading needs to read as its subsection rather than as the section title, and headings cannot be moved.

text: Check 5's cascade states three conditions for its traversal in its own comments, and taking the traversal without them is exactly the failure a copied fix invites. The first is that the visited set is seeded with the root so a citation cycle back to the root terminates instead of looping; the owed closure keeps that seeding verbatim, and it is what makes the fixpoint total rather than merely usually convergent.

The second is that a self-citation is never a dependency. That condition exists at the donor because check 5 reports a list of dependents and a root must not appear as its own. The owed closure reports a set of ids to grade which already contains its seeds, so a self-edge can only re-derive owed-ness a claim already has; the exclusion is not needed here, and saying so is different from silently dropping it.

The third is the one that would have been carried across invisibly. Check 5 excludes ledger claims from its graph, on the stated ground that such an id cannot be a cascade root because it has no typed status, and cannot be a row-to-row dependent because it is not a row. Both properties are artefacts of what check 5 roots at. The owed closure roots at owed-ness under rules 1 through 4, which is defined for ledger claims and for nothing else, and every node in its graph is a ledger claim by construction. So the donor's exclusion does not transfer, and the index this design builds covers precisely the population the donor omitted.
Why the floor is the design and the saving is the side effect

The ticket rests on one measurement, and that measurement was replayed here from TET-30's evidence file rather than taken on trust. It reproduces to the record: 125 records over 35 distinct wordings, 90 repeats, of which 56 are the same workspace filing one record per fact and only 34 are genuine cross-workspace regrades. Seven of those 34 gave a verdict no earlier workspace had given, and all seven moved a claim from supported to qualified. Five arrived from the second workspace to read the wording, one from the third, one from the fourth.

Replaying the scheduling rule against that ledger settles what the floor is for. Ground only what is dirty — one workspace-grading per wording — and the cost falls from 69 gradings to 35 while every one of the seven findings disappears. At N=2 the cost is 51, a 26% reduction rather than the 28% the ticket estimated, and five of the seven survive; N=3 costs 60 and keeps six; N=4 costs 67 and keeps all seven. So the saving and the discovery property trade against each other smoothly, and the confirmation floor is not a safeguard bolted onto a cost optimisation — it is the only part of the rule that preserves what full re-grading was buying. Deleting it, which a later simplification will be tempted to do, converts the feature into the version that finds nothing.

The floor itself stays a parameter, and the replay is why: N=2 keeps five of the seven findings, N=3 keeps six for nine more gradings, and there is no value at which the trade stops being a trade. That is a judgement about a particular memo's stakes, not a constant. But a parameter is exactly the invisible configuration TET-46 objected to, so the value in force is printed in the brief beside the owed list. A reader of the brief, and a grounder acting on it, can then see which floor produced this schedule rather than having to know how the call was made.
why: The paragraph asserted "N=2 retained five of seven discoveries" while citing only C16, which says nothing about the measurement; F16's replay and C23 now establish those numbers, so the sentence is rewritten to rest on a claim that carries it.

text: The rule as decided

A claim is owed when nothing has graded it at all, when everything that graded it graded other words, when the pin its records were taken against is not the pin the memo now states, when fewer than N distinct non-author workspaces have graded the wording it carries now, or when its proposition cites a claim that is itself owed. The last is computed to a fixpoint. The sections that follow take each condition in turn and show where it already exists in the crate, since four of the five are a restriction or a reuse of something `analyze_ledger`, `grounding_provenance` or the citation scanner already computes, and every one of them is decidable from the memo, the evidence file beside it and the snapshot beside that.
What is measured, and what is only argued

The ticket asks for four pieces to ship together, and it is worth being exact about the standing of each. Only the confirmation floor's necessity is measured: strip it and the replayed rule keeps none of the seven findings. Pin detection, the textual closure and the visibility line are argued in this memo from what the code does, and nothing measures what their absence would cost. Extending the floor's evidence to cover them would be the easiest way for this design to sound better than it is, so it does not.

The exclusion the ticket insists on survives contact with rule 5. Making owed-ness propagate through proposition text might look like it needs the claim-to-claim dependency graph that the ticket keeps out of scope, but it does not: the edges are read out of the propositions at schedule time by the same scanner the cascade already uses, from artifacts the memo carries. Nothing in this design asks an author to re-evaluate a dependent, and nothing in it requires that machinery to exist.

A grounding pass is handed a memo path and a workspace name and nothing else, on purpose, so an owed list is only a viable surface if the memo carries everything the predicate reads. It does. The `check` driver already assembles exactly this set from the memo path: the claims and their pins out of the document, the records out of the evidence file beside it, and the authoring identity out of the snapshot directory beside that. It opens no authoring workspace. Nothing in the owed predicate is knowledge only the author has, so the grounder computes its own schedule from the same artifacts a reader could — which is what makes the next question, whether the schedule should be requested or simply emitted, a live one at all.
why: The paragraph named `--owed` as a flag, which the memo later rejects; reworded to match, and given a forward transition to the flag-versus-default section.

text: The ticket asks whether the fix for the pin defect is to digest the pin or to compare it separately. Neither, as it turns out: there is nothing to compare. A fact's pin is a content fingerprint — a sha256 over each observation's label, world markers and output — so two facts minted in one checkout at one commit pin differently whenever their text differs, and it is not a tree identifier at all. A claim's pin is a backticked token lifted from prose, and running the tool's own brief over all five memos this project has rendered returns 87 claims of which not one carries a pin, this memo included. Rule 3 as the ticket states it would compare a value of one kind against a value of another kind that is never present. Shipped as written it is either dead code or, if the absent operand is read as a mismatch, a rule that holds every claim owed forever and gives back the entire saving.
why: C6 was refuted on both operands — F17 shows the fact pin is a content fingerprint rather than a tree id, and that no memo in the corpus carries a claim pin — so the paragraph's whole argument, that the information is present and merely unread, was false.

text: The question rule 3 was written for survives its operands, and it has an answer. Every witnessed record's predicate already records the world markers of the tree its pass stood in, and `check` already recovers the authoring side's tree states from the `facts.jsonl` shipped beside the memo. So rule 3 becomes a tree-state comparison: a claim is owed when no record grading its current wording was taken against the memo's own authoring tree state, for the memo's own worktree root. That is an existential over the claim's fresh records, which settles the quantifier the pin formulation left open — not any, all, or the latest of a heap of unrelated hashes. One thing stands in the way, and it is small: the world markers are written into the evidence file and then dropped when a record is read back, so the field has to be carried into `EvidenceRecord` before anything can read it.
why: P12 explained rule 3 as a document-uniform pin comparison; C8 is withdrawn and C27 replaces the rule, so the paragraph now has to carry the replacement rather than the withdrawn one.

text: This is the one disjunct that reuses nothing. text: That divergence is worth naming rather than smoothing over, and it is survivable for a reason specific to what an owed list is. The schedule settles nothing. No value of N marks a claim confirmed, the full brief goes out unchanged whatever N is, and the only thing a different N can change is how much grading gets scheduled. So the owed list does not need to be reproducible from the memo the way a verdict would. What it does need is for the floor in force to be printed by both renderers, so that a pass's own output records which schedule it acted on — otherwise the number is printed for the benefit of the person who just chose it.

The ticket asks whether being under the floor is a finding at all, given that such a claim is scheduled rather than unsettled. It is not a finding, and the visibility requirement is met without making it one: the count of distinct non-author workspaces that graded the wording a claim carries now becomes part of `grounding_provenance`'s output, printed as a bullet in the human-owed partition as its lines already are. That placement hides a trap. The function has three emission states — a claim with no records prints nothing, a claim whose records are all ingested gets a different string with no workspace list, and only the third carries the line about records witnessed in workspaces. A count added to the third alone would be missing from exactly the claims the floor schedules, which is where it would read zero and where it matters most. It goes in all three. What `check` still does not do is compare the count to N: the floor is a scheduling parameter supplied to `brief`, and a comparison printed by `check` would turn a policy setting into a per-claim pronouncement — a document-level verdict assembled one claim at a time.

text: The obvious substitute fails for a deeper reason, and it is the reason rule 3 leaves the predicate entirely. Every witnessed record does carry the world markers of the tree its pass stood in, so a tree-state comparison looks available. But a marker hashes HEAD together with the working-tree delta — chosen that way so two facts taken in one checkout with different uncommitted content are correctly two states — which means it moves on every commit and every edit. A tree state fixed when the memo was authored can never be re-observed by a later pass, and because facts are immutable, re-rendering carries the same frozen markers forward. Any owed condition keyed on tree identity therefore schedules work that nothing can discharge: a red nobody can clear, which is exactly the defect `analyze_ledger`'s own comments describe having had to rebuild that check to escape. So rule 3 is dropped. The predicate has four disjuncts, not five.

text: Dropping the rule does not mean dropping the defect the ticket found. The divergence it names is real, and it has a home: carry the predicate's world markers into `EvidenceRecord` — one field at read-back, in a type whose occurrences span two modules — and let `check` report which tree each grading pass stood in beside the trees the memo's own facts were taken against. Reported, that observation costs nothing and never fails a run; scheduled, it fails every run forever. The distinction between an unclearable truth and a scheduling condition is the whole of what this section learned, and the memo that decided it is a counterexample to both of the rules it tried first.
why: P13 described the cost of a disjunct that no longer exists; the remedy that survives is a report line, which is what C30 carries.

Of the four, the first two are sets `analyze_ledger` already publishes and the fourth reuses the citation scanner; only the floor needs something new, and what it needs is for the digest-matched record set that is currently a local inside `analyze_ledger` to be exposed, so that "graded on this wording" keeps one definition in the crate rather than two.

text: Rule 4 cannot be borrowed as cheaply, and two of its details decide whether it works at all. `analyze_ledger` maintains two record sets that differ on exactly the case the floor is sensitive to: `fresh` requires the digest to equal the current proposition's, while `grading_current` also admits records written before the digest field existed. Grandfathering is right where it lives — treating an undigested record as grading the current text makes the contradiction checks fire rather than fall silent — but a confirmation count is the opposite polarity, and a pre-digest record counted as one of the N would retire a claim from the schedule on evidence that may have graded other words entirely. The floor counts `fresh` only. Since `fresh` is a local rather than a published finding, exposing it is part of the work, and that is preferable to recomputing the comparison in a second place.
why: C24 now records that `fresh` is a function-local `LedgerFindings` does not expose; the paragraph implied the floor could simply read it.

text: The floor needs a count of distinct non-author workspaces that have graded a wording, and the crate already computes one. `grounding_provenance` takes the claim's witnessed records, dedupes their `pass` values, reads the authoring workspace out of the snapshot's identity, and splits the result into how many of those workspaces authored the memo and how many did not. The second number is rule 4's input. Two things have to change. The count is taken over every record bearing the claim's id with no attention to which wording each graded, and the floor must take it over the records matching the current wording alone. And the restriction to witnessed records, which `grounding_provenance` already applies, has to be part of the rule rather than an accident of where the count came from: an ingested record's pass is a string its reporter typed, so a floor that counted those could be discharged by inventing names, while on the witnessed path the pass is the workspace identity itself.
why: An attack pass showed the witnessed restriction was implicit in C9's mechanism but absent from the rule an implementer would build from; C24 now states it and the paragraph should too.

text: The ticket asks whether being under the floor is a finding at all, given that such a claim is scheduled rather than unsettled. It is not a finding, and the visibility requirement is met without making it one: the count of distinct non-author workspaces that graded the wording a claim carries now becomes part of `grounding_provenance`'s output, printed in the human-owed partition as its lines already are. That placement hides two traps rather than one. The function branches by record composition into three states — nothing at all for a claim with no records, a different string with no workspace list when every record is ingested, and only the third carrying the line about records witnessed in workspaces — so a count added to the third alone would be missing from exactly the claims the floor schedules. And inside that third it branches again on whether the snapshot's identity is known, because the non-author count only exists when there is an author to subtract. Where it does not, the line must say attribution cannot be determined here; a zero would assert that no independent pass graded the claim, when what is true is that nothing can tell. What `check` still does not do is compare the count to N: the floor is a scheduling parameter supplied to `brief`, and a comparison printed by `check` would turn a policy setting into a per-claim pronouncement — a document-level verdict assembled one claim at a time.
why: C17 was revised after an attack pass found a second branch axis; the paragraph described only the composition axis and left the identity states saying nothing or, worse, zero.

text: That divergence is worth naming rather than smoothing over. On the correctness axis it is survivable for a reason specific to what an owed list is: the schedule settles nothing, no value of N marks a claim confirmed, and the full brief goes out unchanged whatever N is. On the discovery axis it is not benign at all, because the amount of grading scheduled is precisely the quantity the replay measures as deciding whether the seven findings survive. Two obligations follow. The floor in force must be printed by both renderers, so a pass's own output records which schedule it acted on rather than the number being printed for the benefit of whoever just chose it. And the default must be stated: both front ends reach the brief today with no floor argument at all, so a caller who supplies nothing has to receive a defined value, and that value is 2 — an unstated default of one is the version the replay shows finds nothing.
why: C28 no longer calls the divergence harmless, and C31 adds the stated default an attack pass found no claim carried; the paragraph asserted the weaker position and said nothing about a default.

text: Seven symbols, each censused across the whole worktree, and the list is longer than the argument above would suggest. A new `owed_claims` occurs nowhere today, so the name is free. `render_text` gains the owed section — but so must `render_json`, because `brief` has two renderers selected by a flag and an owed list added to one leaves the other silent. `brief_file` itself must change: its entire signature today is a path and a bool, it loads no evidence at all, and it is called from two front ends, the CLI and the MCP server, both of which the floor has to be threaded through. `analyze_ledger` must publish the digest-matched record set the floor counts, which its single call site makes cheap. `grounding_provenance` gains the confirmation count. `EvidenceRecord` gains the world markers the reporting line needs, and its twenty-two occurrences fall in exactly two modules. One symbol is deliberately absent: `BriefItem`. Its three-field shape is what withholds scope from a grounding pass, and no part of this design asks for a fourth field on it — the owed list travels beside the items, not inside them.
why: C19 gained `analyze_ledger` as a seventh target and the `EvidenceRecord` change is now for the reporting line rather than a withdrawn rule 3.

text: The ticket asks for four pieces to ship together, and it is worth being exact about the standing of each. Only the confirmation floor's necessity is measured: strip it and the replayed rule keeps none of the seven findings. The textual closure and the visibility line are argued in this memo from what the code does, and nothing measures what their absence would cost. The fourth piece, pin-change detection, does not ship as a scheduling rule at all — this design found no dischargeable operand for it and moved it to a report. Extending the floor's evidence to cover what is only argued would be the easiest way for this design to sound better than it is, so it does not.
why: Rule 3 is withdrawn as a scheduling rule (C29, C30); the paragraph still listed pin detection among the pieces shipping with the schedule.

text: A grounding pass is handed a memo path and a workspace name and nothing else, on purpose, so an owed list is only a viable surface if the memo carries what the predicate reads. It carries almost all of it. The `check` driver already assembles the claims from the document, the records from the evidence file beside it, and the authoring identity from the snapshot directory beside that. It opens no authoring workspace. The one input that is not memo-derived is the floor N, which the caller supplies — so two passes given the same memo and different values of N compute different schedules.
why: C11's enumeration included the authoring tree states for the withdrawn rule 3 and the claim pins the memo does not carry; the paragraph should list only what the surviving predicate reads.

text: `analyze_ledger` computes both of the first two owed conditions today. A claim with no evidence record at all lands in `ungrounded_claims`; a claim that has digested records and none matching its current text lands in `out_of_proof`. Neither set catches a claim whose records all predate the digest field, because both partitions are taken after those are filtered away — the same grandfathering the next section turns on. The owed predicate takes the two sets as given rather than restating them, which keeps one definition of "graded on this wording" in the crate instead of two that can drift. What it needs in return is the ids: both outputs today are rendered message strings for a reader, so `analyze_ledger` has to report the claim ids alongside them.
why: C4 was corrected after a grounding pass showed the old rule-2 gloss describes a claim that enters neither set, and that these outputs are message strings rather than id sets; the paragraph repeated both errors.

text: The ticket asks whether the fix for the pin defect is to digest the pin or to compare it separately. Neither, as it turns out: there is nothing to compare. A fact's pin is a content fingerprint — a sha256 over each observation's label, world markers and output — so two facts minted in one checkout at one commit pin differently whenever their text differs, and it is not a tree identifier at all. A claim's pin is a backticked token lifted from prose, and running the tool's own brief over every memo this project has rendered turns up not one claim that carries one, this memo included. Rule 3 as the ticket states it would compare a value of one kind against a value of another kind that is never present. Shipped as written it is either dead code or, if the absent operand is read as a mismatch, a rule that holds every claim owed forever and gives back the entire saving.
why: C6 dropped its claim count after a grounding pass found the figure stale; the paragraph quoted the same number.

text: Seven symbols, each censused across the whole worktree, and the list is longer than the argument above would suggest. A new `owed_claims` occurs nowhere today, so the name is free. `render_text` gains the owed section — but so must `render_json`, because `brief` has two renderers selected by a flag and an owed list added to one leaves the other silent. `brief_file` itself must change: its entire signature today is a path and a bool, it loads no evidence at all, and it is called from two front ends, the CLI and the MCP server, both of which the floor has to be threaded through. `analyze_ledger` must publish the digest-matched record set the floor counts, and the ids of the two sets rules 1 and 2 read, which its single call site makes cheap. `grounding_provenance` gains the confirmation count. `EvidenceRecord` gains the world markers the reporting line needs, and it is named on twenty-two lines across exactly two modules. One symbol is deliberately absent: `BriefItem`. Its three-field shape is what withholds scope from a grounding pass, and no part of this design asks for a fourth field on it — the owed list travels beside the items, not inside them.
why: C19's census unit was corrected to lines, and C4 now also requires `analyze_ledger` to report ids, which belongs in the implementer's list.

text: Dropping the rule does not mean dropping the defect the ticket found. The divergence it names is real, and it has a home: carry the predicate's world markers into `EvidenceRecord` — one field at read-back, in a type named on twenty-two lines across two modules — and let `check` report which tree each grading pass stood in beside the trees the memo's own facts were taken against. Reported, that observation costs nothing and never fails a run; scheduled, it fails every run forever. The distinction between an unclearable truth and a scheduling condition is the whole of what this section learned, and the memo that decided it is a counterexample to both of the rules it tried first.
why: C30's census unit was corrected from occurrences to lines.

text: The obvious substitute is a tree-state comparison, and every witnessed record does carry the world markers of the tree its pass stood in. The question is whether a later pass can ever satisfy it. It can, but only for a while. A marker is a deterministic function of HEAD and the working-tree delta, and recomputing it at the pinned commit with a clean tree reproduces this memo's own facts' marker byte for byte. At the next commit that stops being true, permanently: the authoring markers are frozen in immutable facts and re-rendering carries them forward, so nothing a later pass does can match them again. Four of the five memos in this repository are already there. A condition satisfiable until the next commit and unsatisfiable forever after is not a schedule; it is the red nobody can clear that the crate's own comments name as the defect that forced its stale-record partition to be rebuilt. So rule 3 is not in the owed predicate, and the predicate has four disjuncts.
why: C29's ground changed after F24 showed markers do reproduce at a clean pinned checkout; the paragraph asserted a flat impossibility the claim no longer carries.

text: Whether it should instead be schedulable is a question this design stops on rather than answers. It has now been decided three ways — a pin comparison, a tree-state schedule, a report — and each reversal came from a real observation, but the last two point in opposite directions and neither is wrong. A memo under active work has a reproducible marker; a memo whose repository has moved on never will again. Choosing a fourth time under no new evidence would be the same process that produced the first three. What would settle it is a measurement nobody here can take: how long a memo's grounding rounds run relative to commits landing on its worktree, across more designs than this repository holds.

The ticket frames rule 5 as matching something like `C\d+` inside prose an author wrote, and worries about false positives. The first answer this design reached was to reuse `citation_ids_in`, the crate's existing matcher for row-to-row edges, on the grounds that it is already the definition of a citation edge and its documented failure mode is a false positive rather than a missed one. Measurement killed that answer. Across all five rendered memos, ninety claims, not one proposition contains a bracketed citation-shaped id — while unbracketed references to a sibling claim do exist in two of them, this memo's own C4 naming C5 among them. A closure built on the citation matcher fires on nothing that has ever been written here, which is precisely the standard this design used to kill rule 3, and it would have shipped as one of the decided rules.
why: C12 now decides the matcher differently after F24 showed the citation-shape matcher makes the closure inert on the whole corpus; the paragraph argued for the matcher that was replaced.

text: So the closure matches against the ledger rather than against a shape. A token in a proposition is an edge when it is byte-equal to an id this document's ledger defines and is not the claim's own. No heuristic decides what looks like an id, because the set of real ids is right there in the document, and nothing can be invented that does not exist. The error direction is false positives — a proposition mentioning a sibling id in passing schedules one extra grading, which settles nothing — and the residual miss is narrow and stated: a claim referred to by description rather than by id is not an edge, and making it one would mean reading prose for meaning. That is a different bound from the citation check's, deliberately, because the two ask different questions: one asks whether a document cites an id, the other whether a proposition names a claim of this ledger.
why: C12 and C13 were both rewritten around ledger-id matching; the paragraph described the bound of the matcher that was replaced.

text: The floor needs a count of distinct non-author workspaces that have graded a wording, and the crate already computes one. `grounding_provenance` takes the claim's witnessed records, dedupes their `pass` values, reads the authoring workspace out of the snapshot's identity, and splits the result into how many of those workspaces authored the memo and how many did not. The second number is rule 4's input. Two things have to change. The count is taken over every record bearing the claim's id with no attention to which wording each graded, and the floor must take it over the records matching the current wording alone. And the restriction to witnessed records has to be part of the rule rather than an accident of where the count came from: an ingested record's pass is a string its reporter typed, so a floor counting those could be discharged by naming alone.
why: C24's justification for "witnessed" was narrowed after F25 showed a workspace identity does not certify a distinct reader; the paragraph carried the stronger reading.

text: It is worth being blunt about what that count guarantees, because the word "independent" invites more than the mechanism delivers. A workspace identity is minted on first use of a name its caller chose, and the crate defines an independent grounding pass as simply a fresh workspace. What a distinct witnessed pass certifies is that separate grounds were captured under a separate identity — a distinct capture effort, not a distinct reader. That is weaker than independence, and it is still the property the replay measured, because the workspaces that produced those seven discoveries did capture their own grounds. The floor should be described as what it counts.

Replaying the scheduling rule against that ledger is what shows the floor is load-bearing, but one figure has to be set aside first. That a floor of one retains none of the seven findings is true by construction: a discovery is a verdict no earlier workspace gave, so it cannot occur at the first workspace to read a wording, on this ledger or on any other. The measurement that means something is what happens above one. Seven substantive verdict changes occurred at all; five of them arrived from the second workspace, one from the third, one from the fourth; and capping distinct workspaces per wording costs 35, 51, 60 and 67 gradings at N of one to four, against 69 unbounded. So N=2 buys five of the seven for sixteen gradings, and every further step buys less for more. The floor is not a safeguard bolted onto a cost optimisation — it is the part of the rule that decides how much of what full re-grading was buying survives.
why: C23 was rewritten after an attack pass showed the N=1 headline is definitional; the paragraph led with exactly that figure as though it were a finding.

text: One asymmetry the design cannot close, and should not hide. Every figure in the replay counts gradings not performed, and a grading is not performed only if some pass declines to perform it. Nothing here makes that happen. A brief emits an id, a proposition, an optional pin and a withheld scope per claim, with no instruction prose in either renderer, and the invariant that keeps every claim in the list is the same one this design refused to touch. The owed section is therefore an artifact a pass may act on, not a mechanism that reduces what it grades — while the costs of building it, threading a floor through two front ends and widening three functions and a record type, are unconditional. The saving is real only if passes use the list, and no claim here says they will, because nothing in this repository could check it.

The ticket asks for four pieces to ship together, and it is worth being exact about the standing of each. One is measured: the replay's ordinal distribution and cost curve say what a floor of two buys and at what price. That is not the same as the figure the earlier draft of this memo led with — that a floor of one finds nothing — which follows from how a discovery is defined rather than from anything this ledger did. The closure and the visibility line are argued in this memo from what the code does, and nothing measures what their absence would cost. The fourth, pin-change detection, does not ship as a scheduling rule at all. Extending the measurement's standing to what is only argued would be the easiest way for this design to sound better than it is, so it does not.
why: C25 was rewritten after an attack pass showed the memo named the one definitional figure as its measurement.

text: The blast radius of that extension is small, and the way this memo first got it wrong is worth keeping. By identifier, `grounding_provenance` is named in three files: its definition, field and zero-init in `checks.rs`, one call site in `lib.rs`, one printing loop in `report.rs`. From that this design concluded no test depends on its wording, which is false. Grep the strings the function emits rather than its name and two end-to-end test files appear, asserting on `SELF-GROUNDED` and on `cannot be determined from here`, one of them asserting the latter's absence. They are substring assertions and an appended count would probably survive them, but that is luck, not the census's doing. A census enumerates a symbol's occurrences and is silent about everything that depends on what the symbol produces — its own declared blind spot, and this memo walked into it.
why: C18 was corrected after a grounding pass falsified its no-dependents clause; the paragraph stated the false conclusion as a bounded fact.

why: C4 was corrected after a grounding pass showed `ungrounded_claims` already carries ids; the paragraph asked for id reporting on both sets.

why: C18 now records test dependents on the emitted strings and C4 narrows the id reporting to `out_of_proof`; the implementer's list should carry both.

text: Rule 5, the textual closure, does not ship — and the road to that conclusion is the most instructive thing in this memo, because it is the same road rule 3 took. The first answer was to reuse `citation_ids_in`, the crate's existing matcher for row-to-row edges, on the grounds that it is already the definition of a citation edge and its documented failure mode is a false positive rather than a missed one. Measurement killed that: across the five rendered memos not one proposition contains a bracketed citation-shaped id, while unbracketed references to a sibling claim do exist in two of them, this memo's own C4 naming C5 among them. The second answer was to match tokens against the ids the document's own ledger defines, which catches those. That died too, on a population the first one serves: the importer's own fixture carries a proposition reading "`foo` returns **4** always [X-2]", and its ids are hyphenated, so a punctuation-delimited token can never equal one.
why: C12 and C13 are withdrawn and C35 defers the closure; the paragraph argued for the second matcher as though it were the decision.

text: So neither matcher covers both populations the tool serves, and the yield on either is small: three real edges across every memo this repository has produced. This design applied a standard to rule 3 — a rule that fires on nothing ever written here is not worth shipping — and it would be dishonest not to turn the same standard on a disjunct that carries a new reverse index, a traversal and a transplant of borrowed machinery to schedule three edges. The closure is deferred, and what it owes before it returns is a statement of its yield on a population some matcher actually works on. That leaves the predicate at three disjuncts: never graded, graded against other words, and under the floor.
why: C13 is withdrawn and C35 carries the deferral; the paragraph stated a bound of the matcher this design no longer chooses.

text: One thing is worth recording about the machinery the closure would have needed, since it was built and then set aside. Check 5 already indexes the reverse citation graph and walks it breadth-first with a visited set seeded by the root, precisely so a citation cycling back terminates instead of looping, and that traversal transfers to a fixpoint over owed-ness cleanly — its two stated preconditions, that a self-citation is not a dependency and that ledger claims are excluded, both turn out not to bind at that destination. None of that is wrong. It simply has nowhere to land while the closure is deferred, which is why this memo carries no transplant.
why: C14, C20 and C21 are withdrawn with transplant X1; the paragraph presented the traversal as part of a rule that ships.

text: The exclusion the ticket insists on holds, and more simply than the earlier draft argued. With the closure deferred, every disjunct that ships reads only records filed against a claim's own id, so grounding scheduling needs no edge between claims at all. Nothing here asks an author to re-evaluate a dependent, and nothing here requires that machinery to exist.
why: C26 is withdrawn for naming a matcher the design rejected; C36 reaches the same out-of-scope conclusion without depending on one.

text: Two smaller corrections belong on the record, because both were things this memo asserted and had taken off it.
why: P35 described the first transplant premise; X1 is withdrawn with the deferred closure, so the paragraph's subject no longer exists and it now introduces the two remaining corrections.

text: The first is the floor's marginal price, which this memo asserted falls away and does not. On the replayed ledger, going from two to three costs nine gradings for one further discovery and from three to four costs seven for the last one — so the step that buys the final finding is the cheapest of them, not the dearest.
why: C20 is withdrawn with transplant X1, and an attack pass showed the diminishing-returns clause false at the step the default turns on; the paragraph's subject is replaced by the correction that matters.

text: A claim is owed when nothing has graded it at all, when everything that graded it graded other words, or when fewer than N distinct non-author workspaces have graded the wording it carries now. That is three conditions where the ticket proposed five. The section on the pin rule explains why one of the missing two cannot exist, and the section on the closure why the other is deferred rather than dropped.
